name: Pro-innovation bias
statement: Rogers's charge is that diffusion research implies every innovation should reach everyone, quickly, unaltered and unrejected, and so mostly studies the ones that did.
meaning: The claim is about a research literature, not about a person. Rogers defines it as "the implication of most diffusion research that an innovation should be diffused and adopted by all members of a social system, that it should be diffused more rapidly, and that the innovation should be neither re-invented nor rejected". He adds that the bias is seldom stated outright in diffusion publications, and is instead assumed and implied, which he calls what makes it troublesome. The consequences he lists are gaps in the record. Ignorance about innovations goes unstudied, rejection and discontinuance are underweighted, re-invention is overlooked, and programmes designed to stop a harmful innovation spreading are ignored. Rogers puts it first among four criticisms of his own field, beside the individual-blame bias, the recall problem and the issue of equality. His explanation is a research habit rather than enthusiasm. A successful diffusion leaves a rate of adoption that can be reconstructed afterwards, and a failed one leaves nothing to count.

origin.where: Diffusion of Innovations, third edition, The Free Press
origin.note: The section "The Pro-Innovation Bias of Diffusion Research" is listed in the chapter 3 contents at page 92, first of four criticisms, and the next of them, the individual-blame bias, is listed at page 103. The third edition carries copyright dates of 1962, 1971 and 1983, and is a revised edition of Communication of Innovations, second edition, 1971. Rogers dates the recognition earlier than the analysis: he writes that the problem "was one of the first biases to be recognized (Rogers with Shoemaker, 1971, pp. 78-79)". That 1971 volume was not opened for this entry, so whether the phrase itself appears in it is unsettled.

evidence: Rogers offers reasons and a tally rather than a measured effect. The tally is Table 2-3 of the third edition, a content analysis of 6,811 generalisations drawn from the 1,084 empirical diffusion publications available in 1968. Variables related to individual innovativeness account for 58% of those generalisations. Consequences of an innovation account for 0.2%. Communication channel use takes 7%, earliness of knowing 5%, opinion leadership 3%, the rate of adoption of innovations across different social systems 2%, the rate of adoption of different innovations within one system 1%, and who interacts with whom less than 1%. Rogers reports 3,085 diffusion publications available in 1981 and gives his impression, from reading them, that the shares had not moved much since 1968. Part of his explanation is historical. Ryan and Gross studied Iowa hybrid corn, and Rogers writes of that innovation's "overwhelming relative advantage" over open-pollinated seed, arguing that copying the design fixed the assumption that other innovations would be similarly beneficial. He then names two causes. Change agencies fund much of the research and are in the business of promoting innovations. And a successful diffusion leaves a rate of adoption that can be investigated afterwards, while an unsuccessful one leaves no visible traces. The choice of innovation is the route by which the bias creeps in, and there he gives two ways: a sponsor arrives with an innovation already in mind, or the researcher picks one with a relatively rapid rate of adoption, because such innovations look noteworthy and are more likely to carry policy implications. The one direct test located is Karch, Nicholson-Crotty, Woods and Bowman's pooled event history analysis of interstate compacts in the United States. Compacts open to all fifty states give an entire universe of cases, with unusually wide variability in adoption patterns. Their abstract reports that limiting diffusion research to widely adopted policies affects the results of previous studies. Scholars are led to overestimate geographic diffusion pressures and policy attributes, and to underestimate professional associations and the chance to learn from previous adoptions. They conclude that the longstanding concerns seem warranted. The article is closed at the publisher, so nothing beyond that abstract is quoted here.

replication.headline: There is no experiment to repeat. Rogers named a habit in a research literature, and the one direct test located, on United States interstate compacts, reports that the habit changes what diffusion studies conclude.
replication.detail: Searches on 21 September 2026 of Crossref, OpenAlex, Europe PMC, the Internet Archive and general web search located no study measuring a pro-innovation bias as an effect in individual judgement. Crossref's bibliographic index returns mainly humanities chapters, 21 of the first 25 hits belonging to one 2017 Edward Elgar volume, Critical Studies of Innovation. Europe PMC returned 65 records containing the phrase. Among them is Smith, Zhang and Colwell, who measured the Giant Texas SmokeScream, a school smoking curriculum, on 512 middle-grade students. Their abstract reports that the data indicated the programme had no effect on students, and that the programme remained popular with schools. They present it as an illustration of what Rogers labelled pro-innovation bias, not as a test of it. Baumann and Martignoni model the idea instead of measuring it. They place firms that differ in an evaluation bias on NK performance landscapes, let them search for 500 periods, and repeat each experiment over 5,000 landscapes. Their abstract reports that the bias can raise long-run performance in complex and stable environments, can lower it substantially when too pronounced, and loses to unbiased evaluation under most other conditions. Those are simulated firms rather than people. Karch and colleagues test the consequence Rogers predicted, in one field, rather than repeating a study of his. OpenAlex's search endpoint returned HTTP 429 on the day of this check, so its ranked result list was not re-read.

limits: This is a critique of a field, and it carries no rate, no magnitude and no population. Table 2-3's percentages describe what diffusion scholars chose to write about, not how wrong they were, and Rogers's own text on page 115 cites Table 2-2 for a figure Table 2-3 holds, giving it there as about 60 percent of diffusion researches against the table's 58 percent of generalisations. The book also uses 3,085 in two senses. Page 46 gives it as the total of diffusion publications available in 1981, of which about 2,297 are empirical reports and 788 other writings, while the footnote to Table 2-3 calls all 3,085 empirical. The 1968 content analysis behind the percentages is fifteen years older than the edition printing them, and Rogers extends it to 1981 on the strength of his impression from reading the later studies. Four documents were not obtained, each retried on 21 September 2026. The second edition, Communication of Innovations, is lending-restricted at the Internet Archive under three identifiers, whose full text returns HTTP 401; HathiTrust returns a bot challenge rather than a paywall, and the Google Books API returns HTTP 429 for exceeded quota. So the 1971 pages Rogers cites were not read. Karch and colleagues' paper is closed access, Unpaywall lists no open copy, the publisher's own page returns a bot challenge, and every claim about it here comes from the abstract, read at Crossref and at the University of Minnesota research portal. Downs and Mohr is listed as green open access by OpenAlex, Unpaywall and Semantic Scholar, all three pointing at one repository record at eduq.info. Unpaywall gives that record no file, its landing page returns a bot challenge, and JSTOR returns one too, so only the passage Rogers quotes is used here. Rogers's 1976 Journal of Consumer Research paper, "New Product Adoption and Diffusion", is listed closed by Unpaywall and by Semantic Scholar and the publisher's page returns a bot challenge, so whether the phrase predates 1983 in his own published work is open. The fourth and fifth editions were not read, so the wording quoted here is the third edition's and later printings may differ. No psychology-specific database such as PsycINFO was searched, so the absence recorded above is a statement about the places named and not about the whole literature.
misreadings: The bias has been rewritten as a feeling. Wikipedia's list of cognitive biases defines it as "the tendency to have an excessive optimism towards an invention or innovation's usefulness throughout society, while often failing to identify its limitations and weaknesses", with no citation attached. The standalone Wikipedia article adds that an innovation's champion holds the bias so strongly they cannot see its weaknesses. Rogers's definition names no person. It names an implication carried by a body of published research, and his causes are funding, sampling and the absence of data on failures. Read as individual optimism, the idea also collides with measured work pointing the other way. Mueller, Melwani and Goncalo gave 73 participants an Implicit Association Test setting creativity against practicality. Those told extra pay would be settled by a random lottery rather than by performance scored 0.15 on implicit bias against creativity, against minus 0.23 for the baseline group, F(1, 70) = 13.13, p = .001, with condition accounting for 11% of the variance. In a second experiment on 140 undergraduates, those asked to argue that every problem has one correct solution rated a novel running shoe 5.06 on a seven-point creativity scale, against 5.76 for those asked to argue that every problem has more than one, F(1, 137) = 15.48. That is people marking novelty down, not up. A second error is to read Rogers as saying innovations are bad. He argues that rejection, discontinuance and re-invention may be rational from the adopter's point of view, and asks for research designs that can see them. He goes as far as calling for some studies with an "anti-innovation bias" to correct the balance of the literature. A third is to assume the label always carries his meaning. Baumann and Martignoni attach it to a firm's own tendency to overvalue new decision alternatives, and Ferreira, von Schönfeld, Tan and Papa cite Sveiby, Gripenberg and Segercrantz for the term, their 107-item reference list carrying no Rogers entry. A fourth is to treat the bias as settled by demonstration. Outside Karch and colleagues' compacts analysis, the searches for this entry found the phrase used as a label for a worry rather than as something anyone had quantified.

Source for every quotation and every percentage above. Table 2-3's percentages are set as an image and were read off the rendered page.

Closed access, and the publisher's page returns a bot challenge rather than a paywall; described here from the abstract, read at Crossref and at the University of Minnesota research portal.

Abstract read at Europe PMC, which lists the full text as subscription-only; source for the 512 students and the null result.

Mueller, J. S., Melwani, S., & Goncalo, J. A. (2012). The Bias Against Creativity: Why People Desire but Reject Creative Ideas. Psychological Science, 23(1), 13-17. Read in full in the published article at the URL below, and every figure confirmed against the accepted manuscript in Cornell's eCommons repository.

Quoted by Rogers in the passages read above, both on the bias and on the instability of diffusion generalisations. OpenAlex, Unpaywall and Semantic Scholar all list it as green open access at one eduq.info repository record; that record carries no file in Unpaywall and its page returns a bot challenge, as does JSTOR, so the paper itself was not obtained.

Listed closed by Unpaywall and by Semantic Scholar, and the Oxford Academic page returns a bot challenge, so the text was not obtained and nothing here is taken from it.

Read in full from the publisher's file server at the URL below, the article page itself returning an edge-server Access Denied; cited as an example of how the phrase is used, an argument rather than a measurement, and as the source for its attribution of the term to Sveiby, Gripenberg and Segercrantz.

Baumann, O., & Martignoni, D. (2011). Evaluating the New: The Contingent Value of a Pro-Innovation Bias. Schmalenbach Business Review, 63(4), 393-415. Closed at Springer and listed closed by Unpaywall, and read in full from the first author's own page at the URL below; source for the simulation parameters and for the abstract quoted above.
